stances.claim: The JBC disqualification rule for candidates with pending criminal or regular admin cases has been uniformly applied since December 1, 2000 -- amending it mid-vacancy cannot help De Lima because the amendment would only take effect after the constitutional August 27 deadline.
The irony of De Lima's situation: she herself opposed the 2011 Tupas amendment proposal that might have helped her now.

If De Lima can somehow hurdle the disqualification, she stands more than an even chance of being nominated and appointed as the first woman and first outsider CJ (not counting the Yulo Japanese-occupation appointment).

one_paragraph_summary: Using the Hamlet parallel -- 'To disqualify or not to disqualify, that is the question' -- Panganiban explains the legal trap confronting DOJ Secretary De Lima before the JBC. The Corona vacancy of May 29, 2012 must be filled by August 27 (the 90th day, accounting for 31-day months). The JBC's timetable was already delayed by the Chavez petition on the two-Congress-seats issue (temporarily allowing Escudero and Tupas), Escudero's absence from interviews, and a Metro Manila monsoon cancellation. The core problem: the JBC disqualification rule (effective December 1, 2000) bars candidates with pending criminal or regular administrative cases. De Lima, Jardeleza, and Herbosa are covered. The IBP denied De Lima's summary-dismissal request. De Lima asked the JBC to amend or suspend the rule -- citing it as possibly outdated or unconstitutional -- but EO 200 and Tañada v. Tubera (December 29, 1986) require 15 days of publication before any rule amendment affecting public rights takes effect. Any amendment would be effective only after the August 27 constitutional deadline. The column adds an irony: De Lima herself opposed Rep. Tupas's 2011 proposal to allow JBC discretion to exempt deserving candidates, arguing for expedited case resolution instead. The JBC has uniformly applied the rule since 2000 -- former Cabinet members Devanadera and Lotilla were also barred. De Lima can challenge the rule in the SC -- accepting the JBC result or 'taking arms against a sea of troubles' -- but if she can somehow hurdle the disqualification, she would stand more than an even chance of being appointed as the first woman and first outsider CJ (excluding the Yulo Japanese-occupation appointment).
